Analysis: All three experts concur that the patient meets DSM‑5 criteria for a first‑episode, severe Major Depressive Disorder (PHQ‑9 22, ≥5 depressive symptoms, functional impairment, duration >2 weeks). There is unanimous agreement that there are no current suicidal ideations, hallucinations, delusions, or a history of manic/hypomanic episodes, thus no immediate safety concerns and no bipolar red flags identified by Experts A and B. Experts A and B both recommend an SSRI as first‑line pharmacotherapy and evidence‑based psychotherapy (CBT or IPT) with close outpatient follow‑up. Expert B additionally notes that the severity may justify referral to an intensive outpatient program.  

Points of divergence: Expert C raises the possibility of underlying medical pathology (e.g., malignancy, endocrine disorder) given the pronounced weight loss and suggests broader laboratory evaluation (including ECG and cortisol) and cautions about a potential bipolar spectrum presentation despite the lack of overt manic symptoms. Expert C also emphasizes the need for malignancy screening if initial labs are inconclusive, a concern not highlighted by Experts A or B.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, thyroid‑stimulating hormone, vitamin B12, folate, vitamin D, urinalysis, fasting glucose, urine drug screen if indicated, ECG (per Expert C), cortisol level (if indicated), and sleep study referral if obstructive sleep apnea is suspected.  

Conclusion: Major Depressive Disorder, single episode, severe.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Psychiatry  

Recommendations: Initiate a first‑line SSRI (e.g., sertraline 25 mg daily, titrating as tolerated) after confirming no medication allergies or prior adverse reactions; provide patient education on expected onset of effect, common side effects, and the importance of adherence. Begin evidence‑based psychotherapy (CBT or IPT) promptly and consider referral to an intensive outpatient program given functional impairment. Schedule follow‑up visits weekly for the first 1–2 weeks to monitor tolerability and emergent suicidality, then biweekly to assess clinical response, adjusting medication dose at 4–6 weeks as needed. Conduct the comprehensive laboratory panel listed above before medication start; if any results are abnormal, pursue targeted investigations (e.g., ECG for cardiac abnormalities, cortisol for adrenal dysfunction, imaging or oncology referral if malignancy is suspected). Screen for substance use disorders, obtain a detailed family psychiatric history, assess for trauma or adverse childhood experiences, evaluate for obstructive sleep apnea, and explore occupational stressors and job performance changes. Assess the quality and availability of the patient’s social support network and consider cultural, religious, or spiritual factors that may influence treatment engagement. Throughout treatment, monitor for the emergence of suicidal ideation or mood elevation indicative of bipolar conversion, and adjust the treatment plan accordingly.  

Notes: Close coordination with primary care for medical work‑up and ongoing monitoring is essential; ensure documentation of all assessments and patient education materials.

Sex: Male
Complaint: Periumbilical discomfort for 3 days now localized to the right lower quadrant, decreased appetite, mild nausea, one loose stool
Analysis: The clinical picture of migratory pain, anorexia, mild nausea and a mildly elevated white blood cell count together with CT imaging that shows a 14 mm dilated appendix, peri‑appendiceal fat stranding and a small contained fluid collection is diagnostic of acute appendicitis with early perforation. All three experts agreed on this diagnosis and on the need for emergent surgical management by General Surgery. Consensus also identified the patient’s advanced age, type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease as factors that increase peri‑operative risk and influence postoperative care. Points of divergence were noted: Expert C raised non‑operative management with antibiotics as a theoretical option in selected cases, while Expert A highlighted percutaneous drainage as a temporizing measure if surgery could not be performed promptly. Expert B emphasized the utility of additional laboratory markers (CRP, lactate) and bedside ultrasound when CT is unavailable. The differential diagnosis list varied among experts but uniformly included cecal diverticulitis, cecal carcinoma, mesenteric adenitis and other right‑sided colonic pathologies, all of which were excluded by the CT findings.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Contrast‑enhanced abdominal CT (already obtained), complete blood count, basic metabolic panel (including renal function), serum C‑reactive protein, serum lactate, electrocardiogram, pre‑operative cardiac risk assessment (e.g., stress test if indicated), medication reconciliation for antiplatelet/anticoagulant agents, allergy history for iodinated contrast and antibiotics, assessment of frailty and functional status, vaccination status review (pneumococcal, influenza), and intra‑operative cultures.
Conclusion: Acute appendicitis with early perforation in an elderly, diabetic, coronary‑diseased patient requiring emergent operative intervention.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery
Recommendations: Initiate nil per os status and begin intravenous crystalloid resuscitation. Start broad‑spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering gram‑negative and anaerobic organisms (e.g., piperacillin‑tazobactam or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole) after confirming allergy status and renal function; adjust dosing for renal impairment if present. Obtain cardiac monitoring and continue baseline anti‑anginal and antiplatelet therapy, consulting cardiology to determine need for peri‑operative adjustment of antiplatelet or anticoagulant agents. Optimize glycemic control with insulin infusion targeting blood glucose 140‑180 mg/dL. Provide deep‑vein thrombosis prophylaxis and analgesia while avoiding NSAIDs if renal risk exists. Proceed to urgent appendectomy, preferably laparoscopic, with readiness to convert to open or perform intra‑operative drainage of the contained fluid collection; percutaneous drainage may be considered only if surgery is delayed or the patient becomes hemodynamically unstable. Post‑operatively, continue antibiotics until culture results guide therapy, monitor for sepsis with serial vital signs and lactate trends, and assess wound for infection, especially given the prosthetic knee joint. Implement early ambulation, pulmonary hygiene, and wound care; reassess frailty and functional status to tailor postoperative support. Ensure vaccination status is up to date before discharge and arrange follow‑up for cardiac and diabetic management. Document all medication adjustments and allergy information.
Notes: Atypical presentation in the elderly may lack fever or overt peritoneal signs; maintain high suspicion and close monitoring for rapid deterioration. Renal function must be re‑checked before contrast‑based imaging and when selecting antibiotics. Consider prosthetic joint infection risk if bacteremia occurs; maintain aseptic technique and consider prophylactic measures as indicated.

Age: 29
Sex: Male
Complaint: Eye fatigue, dryness, and mild headache that worsen with prolonged computer use and improve on weekends.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for digital eye strain (computer vision syndrome) given the history of extensive screen time, normal visual acuity, intact extra‑ocular movements, and unremarkable anterior segment and fundus examinations. All three experts agreed on this primary diagnosis, the non‑urgent nature of the condition, and the absence of red‑flag symptoms. Consensus also identified the need for ergonomic modification, regular visual breaks, artificial tears, and optional blue‑light mitigation as first‑line measures. Areas of divergence included: (1) follow‑up interval – Experts A and B suggested reassessment in 2–4 weeks, whereas Expert C recommended 4–6 weeks; (2) referral pathway – Expert B highlighted optometry as an acceptable initial referral, while Experts A and C emphasized ophthalmology; (3) diagnostic testing – Expert B and C mentioned formal refraction and tear‑film assessment if symptoms persist, a point not raised by Expert A; (4) differential considerations – Expert A uniquely listed blepharitis and conjunctivitis, which were not emphasized by the others; (5) subtle refractive or binocular issues – Expert C stressed possible latent hyperopia or convergence insufficiency, whereas Experts A and B focused less on this. These differences have been incorporated into the recommendations.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: No immediate testing is required. Consider formal refraction (including cycloplegic if indicated) and tear‑film evaluation only if symptoms do not improve with initial self‑care measures.
Conclusion: Digital eye strain (computer vision syndrome) – a benign, self‑limited condition related to prolonged screen exposure.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology
Recommendations: Perform a comprehensive ergonomic assessment of the workstation, ensuring appropriate screen height, distance, chair support, lighting, and glare reduction. Instruct the patient to follow the 20‑20‑20 rule (every 20 minutes look at an object 20 feet away for 20 seconds) and to take regular micro‑breaks to restore normal blink rate. Encourage conscious blinking and consider the use of artificial tears or lubricating ointment for ocular surface dryness; if the environment is dry, recommend a humidifier. Advise on optional blue‑light filtering glasses or screen filters as adjuncts. Evaluate environmental factors such as air conditioning, fans, and humidity, and address systemic contributors including hydration, sleep hygiene, caffeine intake, stress, and medications that may exacerbate dry eye. Screen for meibomian gland dysfunction and treat blepharitis or conjunctivitis if clinical signs emerge. Provide patient education on proper posture to reduce cervicogenic or tension‑type headache. If symptoms persist after 2–4 weeks of optimal self‑care, arrange a formal refraction and binocular vision assessment (including convergence testing) to identify subtle refractive errors or latent hyperopia. Consider tear‑film evaluation at that time. Refer to ophthalmology for persistent ocular surface disease, refractory symptoms, or any emerging red‑flag signs; optometry may be used as an initial referral for refraction and functional visual assessment. Schedule follow‑up in 2–4 weeks, with the option to extend to 4–6 weeks if the patient reports steady improvement, and advise immediate return if any red‑flag symptoms develop.
Notes: Emphasize that the condition is self‑care appropriate but requires monitoring for progression or emergence of concerning features. Patient education and adherence to ergonomic and visual hygiene measures are critical for resolution.

Age: 56  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Shortness of breath and cough of several days’ duration with recent increase in sputum production; chronic morning productive cough for years, ongoing heavy smoking.  

Analysis: The panel converged on the diagnosis of an acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis, a phenotype of COPD, driven by the patient’s 40‑pack‑year smoking history, longstanding productive cough, and recent worsening of dyspnea and sputum. All three experts agreed that there are no red‑flag features (hemoptysis, fever, weight loss, severe dyspnea) and that the presentation does not require emergent emergency‑department care. Experts A and B recommended that initial management be undertaken in primary care with referral to pulmonology for confirmation of COPD by spirometry after the acute episode resolves, and they did not endorse routine use of systemic corticosteroids or antibiotics in the absence of purulent sputum or fever. Expert C diverged by emphasizing a more urgent evaluation to exclude pneumonia or other serious pathology, advocating immediate spirometry even during the acute visit, and suggesting that oral corticosteroids and antibiotics be considered if clinical signs of bacterial infection emerge. This difference is noted in the recommendations.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Chest radiograph; pulse oximetry (oxygen saturation); complete blood count; viral testing for influenza and SARS‑CoV‑2; spirometry (performed when clinically stable, but may be obtained promptly if resources allow); assessment of vaccination status (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID‑19); basic metabolic panel; body mass index measurement; screening for alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency if indicated; cardiovascular risk assessment (blood pressure, lipid profile, glucose); psychosocial screening for anxiety or depression.  

Conclusion: Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis (COPD) requiring non‑emergent outpatient evaluation and management, with the need for diagnostic confirmation of underlying COPD and exclusion of pneumonia or other serious pulmonary disease.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology  

Recommendations: Obtain a chest X‑ray and pulse oximetry at the initial visit to rule out pneumonia, pneumothorax, or hypoxemia. Perform a CBC and consider rapid influenza and COVID‑19 testing given the seasonal context. Review and update influenza, pneumococcal, and COVID‑19 vaccinations. Initiate short‑acting bronchodilator therapy (e.g., albuterol) as needed for symptom relief. Provide intensive smoking‑cessation counseling and refer to a cessation program. Schedule spirometry to confirm COPD diagnosis and stage disease; if feasible, perform it promptly, otherwise arrange it within 1–2 weeks after symptom improvement. Do not prescribe antibiotics or systemic corticosteroids routinely; reserve antibiotics for purulent sputum or radiographic pneumonia, and consider a short course of oral corticosteroids only if the patient’s dyspnea worsens or if there is evidence of significant airway inflammation. Arrange follow‑up in 1–2 weeks to reassess symptoms, oxygen saturation, and response to bronchodilators; if symptoms persist or worsen, repeat chest imaging and consider urgent pulmonology referral. Assess comorbid conditions including hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and cardiovascular disease; evaluate BMI and nutritional status. Screen for alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency if early‑onset COPD is suspected. Obtain a detailed occupational and environmental exposure history. Screen for anxiety, depression, or other psychosocial stressors related to chronic cough and smoking. Educate the patient on red‑flag signs (new fever, hemoptysis, worsening dyspnea, chest pain) and instruct on when to seek immediate care. After resolution of the acute episode, refer to pulmonary rehabilitation and arrange long‑term pulmonology follow‑up for optimization of inhaler therapy, vaccination updates, and ongoing smoking‑cessation support.  

Notes: Ensure documentation of all counseling points and vaccination status; provide written action plan for COPD exacerbations.

Subclinical specialization: General Medicine

If nasal symptoms persist beyond the typical 7–10 day course or if clear triggers are identified, evaluate for allergic rhinitis and consider appropriate therapy.

Analysis: All three experts unanimously identified the lesions as papular urticaria, an insect‑bite hypersensitivity reaction, based on the characteristic pruritic erythematous papules with central puncta, the recent outdoor exposure, and the absence of systemic signs. Consensus was also reached that the condition is non‑urgent, can be managed with self‑care or routine pediatric evaluation, and does not require specialist referral unless atypical features develop. The experts agreed on the key red‑flag features (fever, spreading edema, cellulitis, lymphadenopathy, joint pain, airway involvement, or systemic allergic reaction) that would necessitate urgent assessment, and on the lack of routine laboratory or imaging studies, reserving skin scraping for suspected scabies. Minor differences emerged regarding follow‑up: Expert A and Expert C recommended no scheduled follow‑up, while Expert B suggested a possible routine reassessment in 3–5 days; the panel leaned toward symptom‑driven re‑evaluation only if red flags appear. All experts endorsed symptomatic treatment with cool compresses, low‑potency topical steroids or calamine, age‑appropriate second‑generation oral antihistamines, and nail trimming. Safety considerations for topical steroids, antihistamines, and insect repellents were uniformly emphasized.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None routinely required; consider skin scraping for mites if scabies is suspected or Lyme serology only with a history of tick exposure and a target‑like lesion.  

Conclusion: The presentation is most consistent with papular urticaria, a benign, self‑limited condition that does not require emergent care.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  

Recommendations: Provide cool compresses to the affected areas and apply a thin layer of 1 % hydrocortisone cream or calamine lotion two to three times daily. Administer an age‑appropriate dose of a second‑generation oral antihistamine such as cetirizine 5 mg once daily or loratadine 10 mg once daily, ensuring the child is older than two years. Trim the child’s nails and encourage avoidance of scratching to reduce the risk of secondary bacterial infection. Educate caregivers to use child‑safe insect repellent containing no more than 30 % DEET or picaridin, applying it sparingly to exposed skin and clothing while avoiding the eyes, mouth, and hands. Advise wearing long sleeves and pants during outdoor activities, performing skin checks after play, and maintaining good skin hygiene. Inquire about pets, standing water, dense vegetation, and recent travel to assess environmental risk factors for mosquito, flea, or chigger exposure, and counsel on reducing these exposures at home. Discuss the possibility of recurrent episodes with seasonal insect activity, especially in atopic children, and suggest keeping a diary of flare‑ups to identify patterns. Counsel caregivers to monitor for red‑flag signs such as fever, increasing redness, warmth, pus formation, expanding lesions suggestive of erythema migrans, or new lesions in typical scabies locations (web spaces, wrists); if any appear, seek prompt medical evaluation. Emphasize that routine follow‑up is not required unless the lesions persist beyond 7–10 days, worsen, become vesicular or bullous, or systemic symptoms develop.  

Notes: No scheduled follow‑up is necessary for this uncomplicated case; re‑evaluation should be symptom‑driven based on the red‑flag criteria outlined above.

Analysis: The panel unanimously diagnosed acute bacterial pyelonephritis with early sepsis, based on dysuria, flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, fever, rigors, and urinalysis showing leukocyte esterase, nitrites, pyuria and bacteriuria. All experts agreed that the patient meets SIRS criteria and therefore requires emergent evaluation and treatment. Consensus also identified the need for rapid stabilization, intravenous broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and inpatient admission. Divergence occurred regarding the primary managing specialty after initial stabilization: Expert A and B emphasized Emergency Medicine as the lead for early resuscitation and antibiotic initiation, while Expert C highlighted Infectious Disease/General Medicine for ongoing antimicrobial stewardship, and Expert B noted a potential role for Urology if obstruction is suspected. Antibiotic selection varied (ceftriaxone, piperacillin‑tazobactam, fluoroquinolones) reflecting local resistance concerns. Imaging preferences were aligned (bedside renal ultrasound first, CT if needed).  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: bedside renal ultrasound, contrast‑enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis (if ultrasound inconclusive or obstruction/abscess suspected), complete blood count with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, serum lactate, blood cultures (two sets), urine culture and sensitivity, procalcitonin (optional), repeat renal function after fluid resuscitation  

Conclusion: The patient has acute pyelonephritis complicated by early sepsis and requires emergent care with admission for intravenous antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, and close monitoring.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Emergency  

Recommendations: Initiate immediate sepsis protocol in the emergency department with aggressive IV crystalloid bolus, antipyretics, analgesia and anti‑emetics. Obtain blood and urine cultures before starting empiric IV antibiotics; choose ceftriaxone or piperacillin‑tazobactam pending culture results, reserving fluoroquinolones only if local resistance rates are low and pregnancy remains excluded. Reassess antibiotic choice within 48‑72 hours based on sensitivities, especially given the patient’s history of recurrent UTIs that raises concern for resistant organisms such as ESBL‑producing Enterobacteriaceae. Perform bedside renal ultrasound promptly; proceed to contrast‑enhanced CT if ultrasound shows hydronephrosis, abscess, or if clinical suspicion for obstruction persists. Admit for continuous vital sign monitoring, serial lactate measurements, and renal function checks to detect progression to septic shock. Involve Infectious Disease early for antimicrobial stewardship and to guide duration of therapy; involve Urology if imaging reveals obstruction, hydronephrosis, or anatomic abnormality. Arrange outpatient follow‑up within 1‑2 weeks with Infectious Disease or Urology, repeat urine culture if symptoms persist, and evaluate for underlying structural causes such as vesicoureteral reflux or voiding dysfunction given the prior two UTIs. Counsel the patient on preventive measures, including adequate hydration, post‑coital voiding, and discuss future pregnancy plans that may influence long‑term antibiotic choices.  

Notes: Monitor for mental status changes, worsening hypotension, or increasing lactate as indicators of septic shock. Document all culture results and antibiotic adjustments. Ensure patient education on signs of recurrence and when to seek urgent care.

Age: 77 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Burning and aching pain on the right side of the chest for 5 days followed by erythema, a maculopapular rash that progressed to clear vesicles, then pustules, ulceration, and crusting; associated headache and malaise.  

Analysis: All three experts unanimously diagnosed herpes zoster (shingles) involving the right thoracic dermatome, most consistent with T3‑T5. Consensus agrees that the condition is non‑emergent but requires prompt outpatient evaluation, ideally within 72 hours of rash onset, and that dermatology (or primary care with dermatology input) should lead management. The experts concur that clinical diagnosis is sufficient in typical presentations and that oral antivirals, multimodal analgesia, and patient education are the core treatments. Areas of divergence include Expert B’s identification of missing assessment items—renal function, drug‑drug interactions, and clear criteria for switching to intravenous antivirals—which were not emphasized by Experts A and C. The additional considerations raised during the Delphi rounds (ocular involvement, immunosuppression, vaccination status, lesion care, and red‑flag neurological or systemic signs) complement the core consensus and highlight potential outlier scenarios that require extra vigilance.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Thorough skin examination with dermatomal mapping; assessment for Hutchinson’s sign (lesions on the tip of the nose) to evaluate ocular involvement; baseline renal function tests (serum creatinine, eGFR) and review of current medications to guide antiviral dosing and avoid interactions; complete blood count if secondary bacterial infection is suspected; PCR or Tzanck smear reserved for atypical or uncertain cases; consider neuroimaging or lumbar puncture only if neurologic deficits or meningoencephalitis are suspected.  

Conclusion: Herpes zoster affecting the right thoracic dermatome (T3‑T5) in a 77‑year‑old man.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  

Recommendations: Initiate oral antiviral therapy (valacyclovir 1 g three times daily, famciclovir 500 mg three times daily, or acyclovir 800 mg four times daily) as soon as possible, recognizing benefit even beyond 72 hours in patients over 50 years. Adjust antiviral dose according to renal function and review for interactions with anticoagulants, digoxin, immunosuppressants, or other relevant agents. Provide multimodal pain control: acetaminophen or NSAIDs for mild pain, gabapentin or pregabalin (or topical lidocaine) for neuropathic pain, and a short course of opioids if pain is severe. Counsel the patient to keep lesions clean and dry, apply gentle barrier dressings if needed, and monitor for signs of secondary bacterial infection (increased erythema, purulent drainage, fever). Educate on strict lesion isolation, frequent hand hygiene, and avoidance of contact with pregnant women, newborns, and immunocompromised individuals. Assess for ocular involvement by inspecting the nasal tip for lesions; if Hutchinson’s sign is present, arrange urgent ophthalmology referral. Evaluate the patient’s immune status (history of malignancy, HIV, chronic steroids, diabetes) to identify increased risk for dissemination; in immunocompromised or severely ill patients, consider intravenous acyclovir and possible admission. Monitor for red‑flag neurological symptoms such as motor weakness, meningismus, or severe headache; if present, obtain appropriate neuroimaging and consider infectious disease consultation. Discuss vaccination history and schedule the recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) after lesion resolution, ideally at the follow‑up visit. Arrange follow‑up in 1‑2 weeks to assess lesion healing, pain control, and emergence of complications; earlier review is warranted if any red‑flag signs develop. If pain persists beyond 4‑6 weeks, refer to a pain specialist for possible neuropathic pain management.  

Notes: The protocol emphasizes early antiviral initiation, comprehensive assessment for complications, and individualized adjustments based on renal function and comorbidities.

Analysis: All three experts agree the patient is in status epilepticus that is life‑threatening and requires immediate neurologic and emergency medicine intervention. Subclinical specialization: Neurology

Age: 31  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Six‑month history of bilateral milky nipple discharge, secondary amenorrhea, headaches, and infertility.  

Analysis: All three experts agree that the markedly elevated serum prolactin (500 µg/L) together with a sellar mass measuring 1.1 × 1.6 × 2.1 cm on contrast‑enhanced MRI is diagnostic of a prolactin‑secreting pituitary adenoma (macroprolactinoma). The clinical triad of galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and infertility, plus the progressive headache pattern, supports this diagnosis. Consensus also holds that there is no acute optic chiasm compression, visual field loss, or signs of pituitary apoplexy, making the situation non‑emergent but requiring timely endocrine management. Points of minor divergence include: Expert A emphasizes close monitoring for possible tumor expansion causing headaches; Expert B stresses the need for formal perimetry despite normal confrontation testing; Expert C suggests macroprolactin (big‑big prolactin) assay to exclude assay interference, though this is rarely needed with such high prolactin levels and clear imaging. Additionally, Expert B recommends a baseline cardiac evaluation before long‑term cabergoline because of a rare valvulopathy risk, while Expert A highlights assessment of other pituitary axes and bone health.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serum prolactin assay (already obtained), thyroid panel (TSH already normal), serum cortisol with ACTH stimulation test, morning free T4, LH, FSH, estradiol, IGF‑1, renal function panel, macroprolactin (big‑big prolactin) assay if clinically indicated, formal automated visual field perimetry, baseline transthoracic echocardiogram, dual‑energy X‑ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan for bone density, detailed family history questionnaire for endocrine disorders, and repeat urine pregnancy test before initiating therapy.  

Conclusion: The patient has a macroprolactinoma causing hyperprolactinemia, galactorrhea, secondary amenorrhea, infertility, and headaches. There is no current neuro‑ophthalmic emergency, but prompt endocrine treatment is indicated to normalize prolactin, reduce tumor size, restore gonadal function, and address associated symptoms.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  

Recommendations: Initiate dopamine‑agonist therapy with cabergoline as first‑line treatment, starting at a low dose and titrating to achieve normalization of prolactin and symptom resolution, with discontinuation if pregnancy is confirmed. Schedule prolactin level measurement every 4–6 weeks until target is reached, then every 3–6 months. Obtain a repeat pituitary MRI with contrast at 3–6 months to assess tumor shrinkage. Perform formal visual field testing at baseline and repeat if any visual symptoms develop or if MRI shows tumor proximity to the optic chiasm. Conduct baseline cardiac evaluation with echocardiography and repeat periodically if cabergoline is used long‑term. Screen for secondary adrenal insufficiency with an ACTH stimulation test and assess other pituitary hormones (TSH/free T4, LH/FSH/estradiol, IGF‑1). Arrange a DEXA scan to evaluate bone mineral density given prolonged amenorrhea. Provide counseling on fertility goals, the expected timeline for menstrual return, and the need for reliable contraception until ovulation is re‑established. Offer psychiatric support for mild depressive symptoms, recognizing they may be hormonally mediated, and advise prompt reporting of side‑effects such as nausea, orthostatic hypotension, or cardiac symptoms. Consider macroprolactin assay only if prolactin levels are discordant with clinical and imaging findings. Document detailed family history for hereditary endocrine disorders.  

Notes: The patient should be advised to avoid dopamine‑antagonist medications and to maintain regular follow‑up with endocrinology. Education on medication adherence and early reporting of visual changes or severe headaches is essential.

winner_protocol:
Age: 44 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Progressive nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, lethargy, and hypotension after viral gastroenteritis with inability to retain oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone  

Analysis: All three experts unanimously diagnosed an acute adrenal (Addisonian) crisis precipitated by missed glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid replacement due to vomiting. Consensus identified the situation as a life‑threatening emergency requiring immediate resuscitation, ICU‑level care, and involvement of Emergency/Critical Care for stabilization together with Endocrinology for definitive hormone management. Red‑flag findings (refractory hypotension, severe hyponatremia, hyperkalemia with ECG changes, hypoglycemia, acute kidney injury, altered mental status) were agreed upon. Divergence occurred in three areas: (1) inclusion of drug‑induced adrenal suppression as a differential diagnosis – retained as a secondary consideration per Expert B; (2) immediate ECG – Expert A initially omitted it, but the majority and the extra considerations emphasized that a 12‑lead ECG and continuous cardiac monitoring are mandatory; (3) CBC – added by Experts B and C and incorporated into the final work‑up; (4) timing of fludrocortisone re‑initiation – Experts B and C specified re‑starting once oral intake is reliable, which is now recommended; (5) adrenal antibody testing – Experts B and C advocated testing if the underlying etiology remains uncertain, and this is included as an optional follow‑up.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: 12‑lead ECG with continuous cardiac monitoring, bedside vital‑sign monitor, intravenous infusion pumps, central venous catheter kit for possible vasopressor access, basic metabolic panel (Na, K, Cl, CO₂, BUN, creatinine, glucose), serum cortisol, ACTH, plasma renin, aldosterone (after stabilization), complete blood count with differential, blood cultures, serum lactate, stool studies for infectious gastroenteritis, and point‑of‑care glucose testing.  

Conclusion: Acute adrenal crisis secondary to primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) precipitated by inability to take oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone during viral gastroenteritis.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  

Recommendations: Administer 100 mg IV hydrocortisone immediately followed by either a continuous infusion (200 mg/24 h) or 50 mg IV every 6–8 h until hemodynamic stability is achieved. Begin aggressive isotonic saline resuscitation (1 L bolus) with 5 % dextrose as needed to correct hypoglycemia and prevent cerebral edema from hyponatremia. Treat hyperkalemia urgently with calcium gluconate, insulin‑glucose infusion, and nebulized albuterol; monitor ECG continuously for arrhythmias. Correct hypoglycemia with IV dextrose bolus and consider a dextrose infusion. Prepare for vasopressor support (e.g., norepinephrine) and place a central line if hypotension persists despite fluids and steroids. Admit to ICU for continuous monitoring of vitals, ECG, electrolytes, glucose, urine output, and renal function with labs repeated every 2–4 hours. Re‑initiate fludrocortisone (0.05–0.1 mg) once the patient can tolerate oral intake; consider a temporary dose increase if sodium remains low. After stabilization, transition to oral hydrocortisone (20–30 mg/day divided) and adjust fludrocortisone dose based on electrolytes and blood pressure. Obtain adrenal antibody testing (21‑hydroxylase antibodies) if the etiology of Addison disease has not been previously confirmed, and measure ACTH, renin, and aldosterone levels for baseline assessment. Perform stool studies to identify the infectious agent and continue appropriate antimicrobial therapy if indicated. Monitor for signs of cerebral edema from severe hyponatremia and treat cautiously. Provide comprehensive patient education: sick‑day rules (double or triple oral steroids during illness, intramuscular hydrocortisone if vomiting persists), supply an emergency injection kit, advise wearing medical‑alert identification, emphasize adequate hydration, and instruct to seek immediate medical care for persistent vomiting, diarrhea, fever, or inability to retain medications.  

Notes: Ensure rapid coordination between Emergency Medicine, Critical Care, and Endocrinology teams. Document timing of all interventions and laboratory results to guide ongoing therapy.

All agreed on aggressive fluid resuscitation, vasopressor support, tight insulin‑driven glucose control, tetanus prophylaxis, and obtaining blood and deep‑tissue cultures. Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Computed tomography of the affected limb (already performed), complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, serum lactate, C‑reactive protein, arterial blood gas, serum ketones and β‑hydroxybutyrate, coagulation profile, blood cultures, deep‑tissue biopsy and cultures obtained intraoperatively, bedside Gram stain of tissue, bedside Doppler or ankle‑brachial index to assess peripheral arterial disease, continuous cardiac and hemodynamic monitoring in the ICU, and, if available, hyperbaric oxygen chamber assessment.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery

Recommendations: Activate the massive trauma/critical care pathway immediately; obtain peripheral IV access and begin aggressive crystalloid resuscitation, adding vasopressors if MAP remains <65 mmHg; draw blood cultures and a set of serum ketones before antibiotic infusion whenever feasible; administer empiric vancomycin, piperacillin‑tazobactam, and clindamycin with dosing adjusted for the current creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL and consider renal replacement therapy if renal function deteriorates; start an insulin infusion to maintain glucose 140‑180 mg/dL while monitoring for diabetic ketoacidosis; give tetanus toxoid or immunoglobulin as indicated; provide broad analgesia and consider adjunctive agents for pain control; obtain a bedside Doppler or ankle‑brachial index to evaluate limb perfusion and guide surgical planning; involve infectious disease early for antibiotic stewardship and de‑escalation; monitor for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and lactate clearance, correcting hyponatremia and electrolyte abnormalities promptly; proceed to the operating room without delay for emergent surgical exploration, extensive fascial debridement, and collection of deep tissue for Gram stain and culture; consider intra‑operative fasciotomy if compartment pressures rise; plan for a second‑look debridement within 24‑48 hours and be prepared for amputation if source control cannot be achieved; post‑operatively, employ negative‑pressure wound therapy, evaluate candidacy for hyperbaric oxygen therapy in centers where available, and coordinate reconstructive surgery (skin grafts or flaps) once infection is controlled; continue ICU-level monitoring for hemodynamics, renal function, and metabolic status until the patient stabilizes.

Age: 20 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Itchy, peeling skin between the third and fourth toes of both feet for 2 weeks, associated with maceration and mild erythema; no pain, swelling, or spread beyond the interdigital spaces.  

Analysis: All three experts unanimously identified the presentation as classic interdigital tinea pedis (athlete’s foot) caused by a dermatophyte, most commonly Trichophyton rubrub. The consensus diagnosis is supported by the patient’s athletic status, daily use of communal showers, and the characteristic interdigital maceration and peeling. Experts agreed that the condition is non‑urgent, suitable for outpatient care, and that dermatology is the preferred specialty for definitive management, though primary‑care clinicians can treat uncomplicated cases. There was full agreement on the key differentials (contact dermatitis, inverse psoriasis, erythrasma, bacterial intertrigo, candidal intertrigo, dyshidrotic eczema), red‑flag signs that would mandate urgent evaluation (severe pain, swelling, fever, rapid spread, cellulitis, lymphangitis, ulceration, involvement of soles or nails), and the first‑line diagnostic test (potassium hydroxide preparation of skin scrapings) with fungal culture reserved for refractory or atypical cases. All experts recommended topical antifungal agents (terbinafine, clotrimazole, or miconazole) applied twice daily for 2–4 weeks as first‑line therapy, and systemic therapy only for extensive disease, treatment failure, nail involvement, or recurrent infection. Follow‑up in 2–4 weeks to assess response and monitor for complications was uniformly endorsed.  

The only divergence arose from Expert B, who noted that the questionnaire lacked explicit guidance on considering candidal intertrigo if there is no response to terbinafine or if satellite lesions develop, criteria for when to obtain a fungal culture, and a brief note on transmission risk to teammates and the importance of environmental cleaning. Expert B also highlighted the need for clear instructions on when to suspect co‑existing Candida infection and how to manage it.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of skin scrapings; fungal culture if no clinical improvement after 4 weeks of appropriate topical therapy or if the presentation is atypical. No imaging or routine blood work is indicated.  

Conclusion: Interdigital tinea pedis (athlete’s foot) due to dermatophyte infection, most likely Trichophyton rubrum.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  

Recommendations: Initiate topical antifungal therapy with terbinafine 1 % cream (or clotrimazole 1 % or miconazole) applied to the affected web spaces twice daily for a duration of 2–4 weeks, ensuring the full course is completed even if symptoms improve early. Advise the patient to keep the feet dry, change to moisture‑wicking socks at least daily, wear breathable footwear, and apply antifungal powder to shoes and between toes. Counsel avoidance of barefoot walking in communal showers and recommend decontamination of personal items (towels, socks, shoes) and, if feasible, use of shoe‑spray disinfectants. Address hyperhidrosis by suggesting antiperspirant powders or clinical management if excessive sweating persists. Instruct the patient to avoid topical steroids unless a non‑infectious dermatitis has been confirmed, as steroids may exacerbate fungal growth. Monitor for secondary bacterial infection (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus) and advise immediate medical review if red‑flag signs develop. Educate the patient on the low but possible risk of transmission to teammates or sexual partners via shared surfaces or footwear, emphasizing personal hygiene and environmental cleaning of shower floors and mats. If there is no clinical response after 4 weeks of topical therapy, obtain a repeat KOH preparation and consider fungal culture; evaluate for possible candidal intertrigo, especially if satellite lesions appear, and treat accordingly with appropriate antifungal agents. Should the infection extend to the nails, become extensive, recur frequently, or progress to a moccasin‑type pattern, refer for systemic antifungal therapy (oral terbinafine or itraconazole) and dermatology follow‑up. Schedule a follow‑up visit in 2–4 weeks to assess symptom resolution, reinforce adherence, and inspect the nails for early signs of onychomycosis.  

Notes: Emphasize adherence to treatment and preventive measures as the most common cause of therapeutic failure. Document any use of topical steroids or other agents that could mask or worsen the infection.
